title: Dakjuk
subtitle: Korean chicken and rice porridge
excerpt: Bone-in chicken thighs are simmered with ginger and garlic until the meat falls away, then the shredded chicken goes back into the pot with rinsed short-grain rice to cook down into a silky, comforting porridge. This recipe serves 4 and takes around an hour. It is eaten as a restorative breakfast or a light meal when someone needs something gentle.
sourceNotes: Juk, the category of Korean rice porridges, has been eaten in Korea for centuries as a medicinal food and as a way to stretch ingredients during lean times. Dakjuk is one of the most common varieties, given to children who are unwell and to adults recovering from illness. It is associated with care and home rather than restaurant dining.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The porridge thickens considerably as it cools. Add a splash of water when reheating and stir over a gentle heat.

glossaryTerms.definition: Juk is the Korean term for rice porridge, made by cooking rice in a large amount of water or stock until the grains break down and the mixture becomes thick and creamy. Unlike congee, Korean juk is often made with whole grains that have been partially broken down rather than fully dissolved. It is eaten as a restorative meal, a light breakfast, or given to those who are unwell.

Dakjuk is the specific rice porridge made with chicken, where 'dak' means chicken and 'juk' means porridge. The chicken is typically simmered whole or in bone-in pieces to build a flavourful stock, then shredded and returned to the pot. The porridge is finished with sesame oil and served with simple toppings such as spring onions, sesame seeds and a pinch of gochugaru.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 1 hour in total.
belongs to the family of Korean
porridges and is one of the gentlest things to come out of the Korean kitchen. The method is simple: simmer the chicken first, shred the meat, then cook the rice directly in the resulting stock.

Rinse the rice until the water runs clear before adding it to the pot. This removes surface starch and allows the grains to absorb the stock slowly and evenly rather than clumping together at the start. Stir occasionally during cooking to prevent the porridge from sticking at the base of the pan.

Place the chicken thighs in a large saucepan with the garlic, ginger and water. Bring to the boil, skim any foam from the surface, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook for 25 minutes until the chicken is cooked through and very tender.
Lift out the chicken pieces and set aside to cool slightly. Remove the garlic and ginger from the stock and discard them.
When the chicken is cool enough to handle, pull the meat from the bones and shred it into pieces with your fingers or two forks. Discard the bones and skin.
Return the chicken stock to the hob over a medium heat. Add the rinsed rice and the shredded chicken. Stir to combine.
Simmer, stirring every few minutes, for 20 to 25 minutes until the rice has broken down and the porridge is thick and creamy. Add more water if it becomes too thick.
Stir in the sesame oil and soy sauce. Season with salt to taste. Ladle into bowls and top with spring onions, sesame seeds and a pinch of gochugaru if desired.

items.symptom: Porridge is too thick and stodgy
items.cause: The rice absorbed more liquid than expected, or the heat was too high
items.fix: Add boiling water a ladleful at a time and stir well to loosen. The porridge should flow slowly when a spoon is drawn through it, not sit solid.

items.symptom: Rice has clumped into solid lumps
items.cause: The rice was not stirred often enough and stuck to the base
items.fix: Stir the porridge every 3 to 4 minutes throughout cooking. Use a long-handled spoon to scrape across the base each time. If lumps have already formed, whisk briefly to break them down.

items.cause: The chicken stock was too dilute
items.fix: Taste the stock before adding the rice. If it tastes weak, reduce it for a few minutes on a higher heat before adding the rice, or add an extra tablespoon of soy sauce at the end.

content.text: Dakjuk is a dish of care. It is what Korean families cook for someone who has a cold, an upset stomach, or who simply needs something easy on the body. It is also eaten as a weekend breakfast when there is no rush. The toppings are simple but make a difference: the green spring onion, the sesame seeds, and a small pinch of gochugaru turn a gentle bowl of porridge into something that looks and tastes deliberate.
